name: 4 Maccabees
sourceNote: Translated fresh from the Greek text of 4 Maccabees in H. B. Swete’s edition of the Septuagint (Cambridge, 1909; public domain), with Brenton’s public-domain English version consulted as a check. The book is a philosophical discourse, written in Greek probably in the first century AD, arguing that devout reason is master of the passions and illustrating the claim with the martyrdoms of Eleazar, the seven brothers, and their mother under Antiochus IV (compare 2 Macc 6–7). Its technical vocabulary is rendered in plain modern English: logismos is “reason,” pathos “passion” or “emotion,” and eusebeia “devotion” or “piety.” Greek kyrios is translated “Lord” and theos “God.” Verse numbers follow the standard English versification; where Swete divides or numbers verses differently, this is noted. This is a draft awaiting scholarly review.

verses.text: Since I am about to set forth a most philosophical argument, namely whether devout reason{a} is sole master of the passions, I would rightly advise you to pay earnest attention to the philosophy.
For the argument is necessary to everyone for knowledge, and besides it includes the praise of the greatest virtue, I mean practical wisdom.{b}
If, then, reason is seen to prevail over the passions that hinder self-control, namely gluttony and desire,
it is shown also to rule over the passions that obstruct justice, such as malice, and over those that obstruct courage, namely anger, pain, and fear.
How then, some might perhaps say, if reason masters the passions, does it not rule over forgetfulness and ignorance? They are attempting a ridiculous argument.

For reason does not master its own passions, but those that are opposed to justice, courage, self-control, and practical wisdom; and it masters these not so as to destroy them, but so as not to give way to them.
I could demonstrate to you from many and various sources that devout reason is absolute ruler over the passions,
but I can prove it far more from the manly virtue of those who perished on virtue’s behalf, Eleazar and the seven brothers and the mother of these.
For all of these, by despising sufferings even to death, demonstrated that reason has the mastery over the passions.

For their virtues, then, it falls to me to praise those men who at this season died, together with their mother, for the sake of nobility and goodness; and for their honors I would count them blessed.

For they were admired not only by all people for their courage and endurance, but even by those who tortured them; and they became the cause of the tyranny over the nation being brought down, conquering the tyrant by their endurance, so that through them their homeland was purified.
But I may speak of this shortly, after beginning with the general thesis, as I am accustomed to do; then I will turn to the account of them, giving glory to the all-wise God.
Our inquiry, then, is whether reason is absolute ruler over the passions.
Let us determine just what reason is, and what passion is, and how many kinds of passions there are, and whether reason prevails over all of them.
Reason, then, is the mind that, together with right living, prefers the word of wisdom.{c}
And wisdom is knowledge of divine and human matters and of their causes.
This wisdom, in turn, is the training of the law, by which we learn divine things reverently and human things to our advantage.{d}
The forms of wisdom are practical wisdom, justice, courage, and self-control.
Practical wisdom is the most authoritative of all of these, for through it reason prevails over the passions.
Of the passions, the two most comprehensive kinds are pleasure and pain; and each of these by nature has its seat also in the soul.
There are many trains of passions that follow pleasure and pain.
Before pleasure comes desire, and after pleasure, joy.
Before pain comes fear, and after pain, sorrow.
Anger is a passion common to pleasure and pain, if one reflects on when it has come upon him.
In pleasure there is also the malicious disposition, which is the most varied of all the passions.
In the soul it shows itself as boastfulness, love of money, love of glory, contentiousness, and envy;
in the body as eating everything, gluttony, and eating alone.{e}
So then, since pleasure and pain are as it were two plants of body and soul, these passions have many side shoots,
Each of these reason, the master gardener, cleanses all around, prunes, binds up, waters, and transplants in every way, and so tames the jungle of habits and passions.
For reason is the guide of the virtues but the absolute ruler of the passions. Observe, then, first of all through the deeds that hinder self-control, that reason is sole master of the passions.
Self-control, then, is mastery over the desires.
Of the desires, some are of the soul and some of the body, and reason evidently prevails over both.
Otherwise, how is it that when forbidden foods tempt us, we reject the pleasure they would give? Is it not because reason can overpower the appetites? I believe so.
Accordingly, when we desire creatures of the water, birds, and four-footed animals, and every sort of food forbidden to us under the law, we abstain because of the mastery of reason.
For the passions of the appetites are restrained, checked by the self-controlled mind, and every motion of the body is reined in by reason.{f}

notes.text: Or “pious reason”; Greek eusebēs logismos, the theme of the whole book.
Greek phronēsis, the virtue of sound practical judgment.
Or “that prefers, with right living, the reasoning of wisdom.” The definitions in vv. 15–18 draw on Stoic philosophy.
Swete prints vv. 16–17 as one verse.
Greek monophagia, apparently selfish eating apart from others; the meaning is uncertain.
Greek “are made to strive for honor,” apparently meaning “are reined in”; the sense is uncertain.

verses.text: And what wonder is it if the desires of the soul for union with beauty are rendered powerless?
It is for this, at any rate, that the self-controlled Joseph{a} is praised, because by reason, with his mind, he gained the mastery over sensual pleasure.
For though he was young and at the peak of desire for intercourse, by reason he nullified the frenzy of his passions.
And reason is shown to prevail not only over the frenzied goading of sensual pleasure, but over every desire.
Thus the law says, “You shall not desire your neighbor’s wife, nor anything that belongs to your neighbor.”{b}
And indeed, since the law has told us not to desire, I could much more readily persuade you that reason is able to master the desires, just as it masters the passions that hinder justice.
Otherwise, how is someone who is by habit a solitary eater, a glutton, and a drunkard re-educated, unless it is clear that reason is lord of the passions?

So, as soon as a person orders his life by the law, even if he is a lover of money, he forces his own character, lending without interest to those in need and canceling the debt when the seventh years arrive.{c}

And if someone is stingy, he is overruled by the law because of reason, so that he neither gleans his harvest fields nor gathers the last grapes from his vineyards.{d} And in the other cases too one can recognize that it is reason that masters the passions.
For the law prevails even over affection toward parents, so that virtue is not betrayed for their sake;
it gains the upper hand over affection for a wife, convicting her when she breaks the law;
it rules over love for children, so that one punishes them for wrongdoing; and it masters intimacy with friends, so that one reproves them for wickedness.
And do not consider it paradoxical when reason, through the law, is able to prevail even over enmity,
so that one does not cut down the cultivated trees of the enemy, but rescues the property of foes for those who lost it, and helps raise up what has fallen.{e}
Reason is shown to master the more violent passions as well: love of power, vainglory, boastfulness, arrogance, and envy.
For the self-controlled mind thrusts away all these malicious passions, as it does anger also; for it is master even over this.
Moses, indeed, when he was angered against Dathan and Abiram, did nothing against them in anger, but settled his anger by reason.{f}
For the self-controlled mind is able, as I said, to win the prize of valor over the passions, altering some of them and rendering others powerless.
Why else does our all-wise father Jacob{g} blame the households of Simeon and Levi for slaughtering the Shechemites as a whole tribe without reason, saying, “Cursed be their anger”?{h}
For if reason were not able to master anger, he would not have spoken so.
For when God fashioned the human being, he planted around him his passions and his inclinations;
and at that time he enthroned the mind, the sacred guide, over all, by means of the senses;
and to the mind he gave the law, by living according to which it will reign over a kingdom that is self-controlled, just, good, and courageous.
How then, someone might say, if reason masters the passions, does it not master forgetfulness and ignorance?{i}

notes.text: “Joseph” means “may he add” (Gen 30:24). See Gen 39:7–12.
Exod 20:17; Deut 5:21.
See Deut 20:19–20; Exod 23:4–5. The Greek of this verse is compressed and its construction uncertain.
Num 16. “Dathan” may mean “belonging to a fountain” and “Abiram” “my father is exalted”; both meanings are uncertain.
“Jacob” is popularly explained as “he grasps the heel” or “he supplants” (Gen 25:26; 27:36).
Gen 34; 49:7. “Simeon” is associated with “hearing” and “Levi” with “joined” (Gen 29:33–34).
This repeats the question of 1:5; the argument resumes in 3:1.

verses.text: But this argument is entirely ridiculous;{a} for reason is shown to prevail not over its own passions, but over those of the body.
For example, none of you is able to cut out desire, but reason is able to provide that you are not enslaved to desire.
None of you is able to cut anger out of the soul, but it is possible to bring aid against anger.
None of you is able to cut out malice, but reason can fight on your side so that you are not bent by malice.
For reason is not the uprooter of the passions, but their antagonist.
This can be reckoned more clearly through the thirst of King David.{b}
For when David had been battling the Philistines{c} all day long and, with his nation’s soldiers, had killed many of them,
then, when evening came, sweating and greatly exhausted, he came to the royal tent, around which the whole army of our forefathers had encamped.
All the rest, then, were at supper.
But the king, being extremely thirsty, although he had abundant springs, could not satisfy his thirst by them.
Rather, an irrational desire for the water that was in the enemy’s territory, growing ever stronger, parched him, and undoing him, burned him up.

Then, when his bodyguards were complaining over the king’s desire, two young soldiers, strong men, out of respect for the king’s desire, armed themselves in full armor and, taking a pitcher, climbed over the enemy’s ramparts.
And escaping the notice of the guards at the gates, they went right through the whole of the enemy camp searching.
And having boldly found the spring, they filled from it the drink for the king.
But he, though burning with thirst, reasoned that a drink reckoned as equal in value to blood was a most terrible danger to his soul.
Therefore, setting reason against desire, he poured out the drink as an offering to God.
For the self-controlled mind is able to conquer the compulsions of the passions, to quench the fires of frenzy,
to overcome in wrestling the pains of the body even when they are extreme, and by the nobility of reason to spurn every domination by the passions.
And now the occasion calls us to the demonstration from history of self-controlled reason.

For when our fathers enjoyed deep peace because of their observance of the law, and fared well, so that even the king of Asia, Seleucus Nicanor,{d} set apart money for them for the temple service and accepted their way of life,
then certain persons, rebelling against the common concord, made use of misfortunes of many kinds.

notes.text: Greek logismos, elsewhere “reason,” here means “argument” or “line of reasoning.”
See 2 Sam 23:13–17; 1 Chr 11:15–19. “David” probably means “beloved.”
Greek “the foreigners,” the usual Septuagint term for the Philistines.
The king meant is probably Seleucus IV Philopator (reigned 187–175 BC; see 2 Macc 3:3); “Nicanor” (“conqueror”) was properly the title of Seleucus I. The confusion is in the text.

verses.text: For a certain Simon,{a} who was a political opponent of Onias,{b} the man who at that time held the high priesthood for life, a noble and good man, after he had failed in every way to do him harm by slandering him to the nation, went off as an exile, intending to betray his homeland.
So he went to Apollonius, the governor of Syria, Phoenicia, and Cilicia, and told him,

“Since I am loyal to the king’s interests, I have come to inform you that many tens of thousands in private funds are stored up in the treasuries of Jerusalem, which have no share in the temple and which properly belong to King Seleucus.”
When Apollonius learned all the details of this, he praised Simon for his concern for the king, and going up to Seleucus he disclosed the treasure of money to him.
And having received authority over the matter, he came quickly into our homeland with the accursed Simon and a very heavy army
and said that he had come by the king’s commands to take the private funds of the treasury.

And when the nation protested at his word and spoke against it, thinking it utterly outrageous that those who had entrusted deposits to the temple treasury should be robbed of them, they hindered him as far as they could.
But Apollonius went off with threats to the temple.
And while the priests, with women and children, were in the temple beseeching God to shield the holy place that was being treated with contempt,

and while Apollonius was going up with an armed host to seize the money, there appeared from heaven angels on horseback, flashing lightning from their weapons, and casting great fear and trembling upon them.

Apollonius collapsed half dead in the temple’s outer court, which was open to all peoples,{c} raised his hands toward heaven, and tearfully begged the Hebrews to pray for him and to placate the heavenly host.
For he said that he had sinned, so that he even deserved to die, and that if he were saved he would sing to all people of the blessedness of the holy place.

Moved by these words, Onias the high priest prayed for him, though he was also on his guard lest King Seleucus should think that Apollonius had been overthrown by human treachery and not by divine justice.
And he, saved beyond expectation, went off to report to the king what had happened to him.{d}
When King Seleucus died, his son Antiochus Epiphanes{e} succeeded to the rule, an arrogant and terrible man,
who removed Onias from the high priesthood and appointed his brother Jason{f} high priest,
Jason having agreed that, if Antiochus would entrust the office to him, he would pay each year about 137 tons of silver.{g}
And he entrusted to him the high priesthood and the leadership of the nation.
And Jason turned the nation aside and changed its citizenship over to every kind of lawlessness,
so that he not only built a gymnasium on the very citadel{h} of our homeland but also abolished the care of the temple.
Divine justice, angered at these things, made Antiochus himself its enemy.
For when he was at war with Ptolemy in Egypt, and heard that a rumor had spread that he had died and that the people of Jerusalem were rejoicing exceedingly, he quickly marched back against them.
And when he had plundered them, he issued a decree that if any of them were seen living by the ancestral law, they should die.
And when he was not able in any way to break down by his decrees the nation’s devotion, but saw all his threats and punishments being set at nought,
so that even women, because they had circumcised their children, were thrown down from heights together with their babies, though they knew beforehand that they would suffer this,{i}
when, then, his decrees were despised by the people, he himself tried through tortures to compel each member of the nation to taste defiling foods and to renounce Judaism.{j}

notes.text: “Simon” (Hebrew Shimon) is associated with “hearing.” Compare the parallel account in 2 Macc 3–4, where Simon is called captain of the temple and the governor is Apollonius, but the officer sent is Heliodorus.
Onias III, high priest about 190–175 BC. The meaning of “Onias” (perhaps Hebrew Honiyah, “the LORD is gracious”) is uncertain.
Greek pamphylos, “of all tribes,” the court open to all peoples; the exact sense is uncertain.
Compare 2 Macc 3:22–40.
Antiochus IV (reigned 175–164 BC). “Epiphanes” means “(god) manifest.”
Jason is the Greek name taken by Jeshua (Joshua), brother of Onias III; “Jason” in Greek suggests “healer.” See 2 Macc 4:7–10.
Greek “3,660 talents”; a talent was ~75 lb (34 kg), so the sum is about 137 tons (124,000 kg). Compare 2 Macc 4:8–9.
Greek akra, “height” or “citadel”; compare 2 Macc 4:12, where the gymnasium is built “under the citadel.”
Compare 2 Macc 6:10.
Greek Ioudaismos; compare 2 Macc 2:21.

verses.text: The tyrant Antiochus, then, seated in state with his counselors on a certain high place, with his armed troops standing around him,
ordered the guards to drag forward each and every one of the Hebrews and to compel them to taste pork and food sacrificed to idols.
And should any refuse to eat what defiles, these were to be racked upon wheels and put to death.

When many had been seized, one, the first from the flock, a Hebrew named Eleazar,{a} a priest by descent, by learning an expert in the law, far along in years, and well known for his age to many around the tyrant, was led forward near him.
And when Antiochus saw him he said,

“Before I begin the tortures against you, old man, I would advise you to taste the pork and save yourself; for I respect your age and your gray hairs, though having had them so long you do not seem to me to be a philosopher, since you observe the religion of the Jews.
For why, when nature has granted it, do you loathe eating the very fine meat of this animal?
It is senseless not to enjoy pleasant things that carry no disgrace, and wrong to spurn the gifts of nature.
And it seems to me that you will act more senselessly still if, holding vain opinions about the truth,
you also despise me, to your own punishment. Will you not awaken from your foolish philosophy,
and scatter the nonsense of your reasoning, and, taking up a mind worthy of your age, pursue the philosophy of what is truly advantageous,
and, bowing before my humane exhortation, have pity on your own old age?
Consider this: even if some power does watch over this religion of yours, it would pardon you for any offense committed under compulsion.”
When the tyrant was urging him in this way to the unlawful eating of meat, Eleazar asked leave to speak.
And receiving permission to speak, he began to address the assembly as follows:
“We, Antiochus, who have been persuaded to live by the divine law, consider that no compulsion is more powerful than our obedience to the law.
Therefore we do not consider it right to transgress the law in any way.
And yet, even if our law were not truly divine, as you suppose, but we only thought it divine, even so it would not be permitted us to make void our reputation for piety.
So do not regard it as a small sin if we should eat defiling food;
for to transgress the law in small things and in great is of equal weight,
since in either case the law is equally despised.
You scoff at our philosophy, as though we did not live by it with sound reason.
For it instructs us in self-mastery, that we may rule over every pleasure and every desire; and it drills us in courage, that we may bear every hardship of our own free will;
and it instructs us in justice, so that in all our conduct we act with equity; and it teaches piety, so that we worship with due reverence the only God who exists.
For this reason we refuse defiling food; because we trust that God established the law, we understand that the Creator of the cosmos, in giving the law, treats us kindly in keeping with our nature.
What will be suited to our souls he has permitted us to eat; what will be contrary to them he has forbidden us to eat as meat.
It is tyrannical of you not only to compel us to transgress the law, but also to eat, so that you may deride us for this defiling food that is most hateful to us.
But you shall not have this laugh at my expense,
nor will I neglect the sacred oaths of my ancestors to keep the law,
no, not though you cut my eyes out and waste my inward parts away.
I am not so old and unmanly that my reason is not made young again by piety.
Against this, make ready your wheels and fan the fire more fiercely.
I will not so pity my own old age that I myself should break down the ancestral law.
I will not play you false, O law my teacher, nor will I desert you, beloved self-mastery.
I will not put you to shame, philosophic reason, nor will I deny you, honored priesthood and knowledge of the lawgiving.
You will not defile the reverend mouth of my old age, nor my lifetime lived lawfully.
Pure will my fathers receive me, unafraid of your compulsions even to death.
Over the impious you may play the tyrant; but over my reasonings on piety you will be master neither by words nor by deeds.”

notes.text: “Eleazar” means “God has helped.” Compare 2 Macc 6:18–31, where he is called a scribe.

verses.text: When he had answered the tyrant’s exhortations in this way, the guards standing by dragged Eleazar roughly to the instruments of torture.
And first they stripped the old man, who was adorned with the dignity of his piety.
Then, tying his arms behind him on each side, they flogged him with whips,
while a herald on the other side shouted, “Obey the king’s commands!”
But the great-souled Eleazar, truly noble, as though being tortured in a dream, was in no way turned aside.
Instead, with his eyes lifted high to heaven, the old man had his flesh torn by the whips, and he streamed with blood, and his sides were wounded through.
And dropping to the earth, since his body could no longer bear the agonies, he still held his reason erect and unbowed.
Then one of the cruel guards leaped upon him and kicked him in the flank to make him get up when he fell.
But he endured the pains, scorned the compulsion, and held out under the abuses;
and like a noble athlete taking blows, the old man was victorious over his torturers.
Indeed, with his face sweating and gasping heavily, he was admired even by the torturers themselves for his good fortune.{a}
So, partly out of pity for his old age,
partly from sympathy, because they knew him, and partly from admiration at his endurance, some of the king’s men approached him and said,
“Why do you destroy yourself so unreasonably by these evils, Eleazar?
We will set before you some of the cooked dishes; you pretend to taste the pork, and save yourself.”
And Eleazar, as though tortured more bitterly by the advice, cried out,
“May we, the children of Abraham,{b} never think so basely that through weakness of soul we would act out a play unbecoming to us!
For it would be irrational, if after living our life in accordance with truth up to old age, and lawfully guarding our reputation for it, we should now change course,
and should ourselves become a pattern of impiety to the young, so as to become an example of eating defiling food.
It would be shameful if we should live on for a little while, and during that time be ridiculed by all for cowardice,
and be despised by the tyrant as unmanly, and not defend our divine law to the death.
Therefore, children of Abraham, die nobly for piety’s sake!
And you, guards of the tyrant, why do you delay?”
Seeing him so high-minded in the face of the compulsions, and not changed even by their own pity, they led him to the fire.
There they burned him with cruelly contrived instruments, threw him down, and poured foul-smelling liquids into his nostrils.
And when he was already burned to the bones and about to faint, he lifted up his eyes to God and said,
“You know, God, that I could be saved, yet I am dying in fiery torment for the sake of the law.
Be gracious to your nation, being content with the penalty we pay on their behalf.
Let my blood be a cleansing for them, and receive my soul as a ransom-life for theirs.”{c}
And having said this, the holy man died nobly in his tortures, and even in the tortures of death he resisted by reason for the sake of the law.
Admittedly, then, devout reason is master of the passions.
For if the passions had prevailed over reason, I would have rendered to them the testimony of their mastery.
But now, since reason has conquered the passions, we fittingly assign to it the authority of leadership.
And it is right for us to acknowledge that the power belongs to reason, since it masters even external pains,{d}
for it would be ridiculous to deny it. And I prove that reason has not only mastered pains, but also masters pleasures and does not yield to them.

notes.text: Greek eutychia, “good fortune” or “success”; the sense here is obscure.
“Abraham” is explained as “father of a multitude” (Gen 17:5).
Greek antipsychon, “a ransom” or “a substitute life”; compare 17:21–22.
Swete numbers v. 35 separately with a mark; the division of vv. 34–35 follows the standard English verses.

verses.text: For like a most excellent helmsman, the reason of our father Eleazar steered the ship of piety on the sea of the passions,
and though buffeted by the tyrant’s threats and swamped by the towering waves of the tortures,
in no way did it turn aside the rudders of piety until it sailed into the harbor of victory over death.

No city besieged with many and varied engines ever held out as did that all-holy man. Though his sacred soul was set ablaze with tortures and racks, he moved his besiegers to defeat{a} through the reason that shields piety.
For father Eleazar, stretching out his mind like a sheer cliff, broke the raging waves of the passions.
O priest worthy of the priesthood, you did not defile your sacred teeth, nor did you let your stomach, which had room only for godliness and purity, share in defiling food.
O you who are in accord with the law, lover of wisdom in a godly life!
Such ought to be those who practice the law with their own blood,{b} and who defend it with noble sweat through sufferings even to death.

You, father, by your endurance confirmed our loyalty to the law so that it was glorified; you did not set aside the holiness you had spoken of with reverence; and by your deeds you made the words of philosophy trustworthy.
O aged man more powerful than tortures, elder more vigorous than fire, greatest king over the passions, Eleazar!
For as father Aaron,{c} fully equipped with the censer, hastened through the multitude of the nation and overcame the angel who brought burning,{d}
so Eleazar, the descendant of Aaron, though melted down by the fire, was not turned aside in his reason.
And yet, most wonderful of all, though he was an old man, with the strength of his body already spent, his flesh slackened all around, and his sinews worn out, he became young again
in spirit through reason, and with an Isaac-like{e} reasoning he made the many-headed rack of no effect.
O blessed old age, reverend gray head, and lawful life, which the faithful seal of death brought to perfection!
If, then, an old man despised tortures even to death for piety’s sake, admittedly devout reason is the leader of the passions.
But perhaps some might say, “Not all prevail over the passions, because not all have prudent reason.”{f}
But those who give thought to piety with their whole heart, they alone are able to master the passions of the flesh,
since they believe that to God they do not die, as our patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob did not, but they live to God.
There is no contradiction, then, in the fact that some appear to be ruled by passions because of weak reason.
For who, living as a philosopher devoutly by the whole rule of philosophy, and having trusted in God,
and knowing that it is blessed to endure every pain for the sake of virtue, would not prevail over the passions through piety?
For only the wise and self-controlled man is courageous and lord of the passions.{g}

notes.text: Greek “he moved the besiegers”; the sense of the verb here is uncertain.
Or “who make the law their craft with their own blood”; the Greek is unusual.
The meaning of “Aaron” is uncertain.
See Num 16:46–48 (Hebrew 17:11–13). Wisdom 18:21–25 also describes Aaron’s victory over “the destroyer.”
“Isaac” means “he laughs” (Gen 21:6). The allusion is to Isaac’s willingness to be sacrificed (Gen 22).
Swete prints vv. 16–17 as one verse.
Or “For only the wise and self-controlled man is courageous and master of the passions.” Swete numbers the next sentence as 7:24; here it is 8:1, following the standard English verses.

verses.text: For this reason, at any rate, even mere youths, living as philosophers by the reason of piety, prevailed over still harsher instruments of torture.{a}

For when the tyrant had been conspicuously defeated in his first attempt, being unable to compel an old man to eat defiling food, then, in a violent passion, he ordered others from among the young men of the Hebrews to be brought; and if they would eat defiling food, they were to be released once they had eaten, but if they refused, they were to be tortured more cruelly.{b}
When the tyrant had given these orders, seven brothers were brought in together with their aged mother, handsome, modest, noble, and accomplished in every way.

When the tyrant saw them encircling their mother in the middle as though in a choral dance, he was pleased with them; and struck by their comeliness and their noble bearing, he smiled at them, called them near, and said,

“Young men, I admire with goodwill the beauty of each one of you; and since I hold in very high honor so large a number of brothers, I not only advise you not to be seized by the same madness as the old man who was tortured before you,
but I also urge you to yield to me and enjoy my friendship. For as I have power to chastise any who disregard my commands, so I have power to do good to any who heed me.
Believe me, then, and you will be given posts of authority in my service, if you will abandon the traditional rule of your way of life;
and sharing in the Greek way of life and changing your manner of living, take delight in your youth.
For if you provoke me by disobeying, you will force me to destroy every one of you with dreadful punishments and tortures.
So take pity on yourselves, for even I, your enemy, feel compassion for your youth and good looks.
Will you not consider this, that nothing awaits you if you disobey except to die on the rack?”
As he said these things, he ordered the instruments of torture to be set out in front of them, so that through fear too he might persuade them to eat defiling food.

When the guards had set out wheels and joint-dislocators, racks and hooks{c} and catapults{d} and cauldrons, frying pans and thumbscrews, iron claws and wedges, and coals for the fire, the tyrant resumed and said,
“Boys, be afraid; and the justice you revere will be merciful to you for transgressions done under compulsion.”
But they, hearing these enticements and seeing the dreadful devices, not only were not afraid but even answered the tyrant with philosophy, and by their sound reasoning destroyed his tyranny.
And yet let us reckon: if there had been some among them who were faint-hearted and unmanly, what words would they have used? Would they not have been these?
“O wretched us, and utterly senseless! When the king is summoning us and calling us to benefits, should we not obey him?
Why do we cheer ourselves with empty wishes and venture on a disobedience that brings death?
Shall we not fear, brothers, the instruments of torture, and weigh the threats of the tortures, and flee this vainglory and ruinous boastfulness?
Let us have pity on our own youth, and have compassion on our mother’s old age;
and let us consider that if we disobey we shall die.
Even divine justice will pardon us if we fear the king under compulsion.
Why do we take ourselves out of this most pleasant life and rob ourselves of this sweet world?
Let us not struggle against compulsion, nor be vainglorious over our own racking.
Not even the law itself would of its own will slay us for being frightened at the racks.
Why has such contentiousness become fixed in us, and why does a death-bringing endurance please us, when we might live in tranquility by obeying the king?”
But the young men, though about to be tortured, said none of these things, nor did they even consider them.
For they were contemptuous of the passions and absolute rulers over pains.
Accordingly, the moment the tyrant stopped urging them to eat what defiles, all of them at once with a single voice, as if from one soul, declared:

notes.text: Swete numbers this verse 7:24.
Swete divides this verse into two (8:1–2).
Greek trochantēres; the exact nature of this device is uncertain.
Greek katapeltai, probably some machine for stretching or crushing; the meaning is uncertain.

verses.text: “Tyrant, what are you waiting for? We stand prepared to perish sooner than break the commands handed down by our fathers.
For we would rightly be ashamed before our forebears if we did not make use of obedience to the law and of knowledge as our counselor.
Tyrant, counselor of lawlessness, do not, while hating us, pity us more than they do.{a}
For we consider your mercy, which offers us safety at the price of breaking the law, to be harder than death itself.
You try to frighten us by threatening us with death through tortures, as though you had not learned from Eleazar a short while ago.

And if the old men of the Hebrews died for piety’s sake after enduring tortures too, we the young would more fittingly die, scorning the tortures of your compulsions, which our aged teacher also conquered.
Make the attempt, then, tyrant; and if you put us to death for piety’s sake, do not suppose that you harm us by torturing us.
For we, through this ill-treatment and endurance, shall win the prizes of virtue;{b}
but you, for the abominable murder of us, will undergo at the hands of divine justice the eternal torment by fire that you deserve.”
When they had said these things, the tyrant was not only angry with them as with the disobedient, but enraged as with the ungrateful.
So, at his command, the scourgers brought forward the eldest of them, and tearing off his tunic, they bound his hands and arms on each side with thongs.
When they had worn themselves out beating him with the whips, accomplishing nothing, they threw him up onto the wheel.
Stretched out on it, the noble youth had his limbs dislocated.
And as he was broken in every limb, he denounced the tyrant, saying,
“Most abominable tyrant, enemy of heavenly justice, savage-minded, you are mistreating me in this way not because I have murdered anyone or acted impiously, but because I defend the divine law.”
And when the guards urged, “Consent to eat, and be set free from the torments,”
he said, “Your method is not so strong, you abominable servants, as to take my reason captive. Cut off my limbs, burn my flesh, and twist my joints;
through all the tortures I will convince you that the children of the Hebrews alone are unconquerable for the sake of virtue.”
As he spoke thus, they heaped fire beneath him, and fanning it into flame,{c} drew the wheel still tauter.
The wheel was stained with blood on every side, and the heap of coals was quenched by the dripping fluids of his body, and pieces of flesh were whirling around the axles of the machine.
And though the framework of his bones was already melting away, the great-souled youth, a true son of Abraham, did not groan.
But, as though he were being transformed by fire into incorruption, he endured the racking nobly.
“Imitate me, brothers,” he said. “Do not desert your post in my contest,{d} and do not forswear our brotherhood in courage. Fight a sacred and noble campaign for piety,
through which our fathers’ righteous providence may show mercy to the nation and punish the accursed tyrant.”
Having spoken so, the youth who was fit for holiness let his soul break away.{e}

While all were marveling at his steadfastness of soul, the guards brought forward the one second in age to the first, and fitting on iron hands with sharp claws, they bound him to the instruments and the catapult.
And when, inquiring whether he would be willing to eat before being tortured, they heard his noble resolve,
those leopard-like beasts tore at him from the sinews with the iron hands and ripped off all the flesh as far as the chin, and the skin of his head. But he, steadfastly bearing this agony, said,
“How sweet is every form of death for the sake of our ancestral piety!” And he said to the tyrant,
“Most savage of all tyrants, does it not seem to you that you suffer worse torment than I, beholding the haughty calculation of your tyranny overcome by our endurance on behalf of piety?
For I lighten my pain by the pleasures that come through virtue,
but you are tortured by the threats that come with impiety. And you will not escape, most abominable tyrant, the judgments of divine wrath.”

notes.text: Greek “do not, hating us, pity us beyond them”; the sense is obscure. “They” may be the forebears of v. 2.
Or “shall carry off the prizes of virtue,” an athletic image.
Or “goading”; the Greek is uncertain.
Greek “do not desert my lifetime” or “my eternity”; the sense is uncertain.
Literally “broke off his soul.”

verses.text: When he too had endured his celebrated death, the third was led forward, being earnestly urged by many to taste the food and save himself.
But he shouted out, “Are you ignorant that one and the same father sired both me and the dead, that one mother gave us birth, and that I was reared in the same doctrines?
I do not forswear the noble kinship of my brotherhood.
Therefore, if you have any instrument of punishment, apply it to my body; for my soul you cannot touch, not even if you wish to.”
But they, taking the man’s boldness of speech bitterly, dislocated his hands and feet with joint-dislocating instruments, and prying his limbs out of their sockets with levers, they dismembered him;
and they wrenched his fingers, his arms, his legs, and his elbows.

And when they were in no way able to strangle his spirit,{a} they tore off his skin, together with the very tips of his fingers, scalping him in the Scythian fashion,{b} and at once led him to the wheel.
Upon it, with his backbone wrenched apart joint from joint, he beheld his flesh shredded all about, and drops of blood streaming down out of his bowels.
And as he was about to die, he said,
“We, most abominable tyrant, are suffering these things for the sake of our godly training and virtue;{c}
whereas you, on account of your ungodliness and your thirst for blood, shall bear torments that never come to an end.”
And once this one too had died as befitted a brother, they hauled up the fourth, telling him,
“Do not you also be seized by the same madness as your brothers, but obey the king and save yourself.”
But he answered them, “The fire you hold against me is not so scorching that I should play the coward.
I swear by my brothers’ blessed death, by the tyrant’s everlasting ruin, and by the famous life of the godly: I will not disown our noble brotherhood.
Devise tortures, tyrant, so that through them also you may learn that I am a brother of those who were tortured before me.”
Hearing this, Antiochus, that devourer of blood, that killer, that most loathsome of men, commanded that his tongue be cut out.
But he said, “Even if you take away the organ of speech, God hears also those who are silent.
See, my tongue is stretched out; cut it, for you will not by this cut out the tongue of our reason.
Gladly, for God’s sake, we let the limbs of our body be mutilated.
But God will swiftly pursue you, for you are cutting out a tongue that sang melodies of divine hymns.”

notes.text: Greek “to strangle him”; the object is probably his resolve, but the sense is uncertain.
Greek apeskythizon, “they scalped,” a practice associated with the Scythians.
Or “for the sake of the training and virtue of God.”

verses.text: When this one also, savagely abused by the tortures, had died in them, the fifth leaped forward, saying,
“Tyrant, I have no intention of begging off from torture on virtue’s behalf.
I have come forward of my own accord, so that by killing me too you may owe to heavenly justice a penalty for a still greater number of wrongs.
You hater of virtue and hater of humankind, for what deed of ours are you ravaging us like this?
Does it seem evil to you that we revere the Creator of all things and live according to his virtuous law?
But these things deserve honors, not tortures,
if only you had perception of human longing and had hope of salvation from God.{a}
But as it is, being estranged from God, you make war on those who are devout toward God.”
As he spoke such words, the guards bound him and hauled him to the catapult.

Tying him to it at the knees and fastening them with iron fetters, they bent his loins back over the wheel’s wedge; and around it he was entirely curled back like a scorpion upon the wheel, and torn limb from limb.
In this manner, cramped in his breathing and choked in his body,
he said, “Fine favors, tyrant, fine favors you grant us against your will, giving us the chance, through still nobler sufferings, to display our endurance for the law.”
When this one too had died, the sixth, a mere boy, was brought. When the tyrant inquired whether he would like to eat and be set free, he said,
“In years I am younger than my brothers, but in understanding I am their equal in age.
For since we were born and raised for the same ends, we are bound to die for the same causes likewise.
So if you have decided to torture those who refuse defiling food, then torture!”
Once he had spoken so, they brought him over to the wheel.
Stretched out on it carefully, limb by limb, and with his spine pulled apart, he was roasted from beneath.
And heating sharp spits red-hot, they applied them to his back; and piercing his sides, they burned his entrails through.
And while being tortured he said, “O contest fit for holy men, to which so many of us brothers have been summoned for piety’s sake to a training ground of pains, and we have not been conquered!
For devout knowledge, tyrant, cannot be conquered.
Armed with nobility, I too shall die with my brothers,
and I myself shall bring down a mighty avenging spirit on you, you deviser of novel torments, foe of all who are genuinely godly.
We six boys have brought your tyranny to nothing.
For is not your failure to change our reasoning, or to force us to eat defiling food, your overthrow?
Your fire is cold to us, your catapults cause us no pain, and your violence is powerless.
For it is not a tyrant’s but the divine law’s guards that stand over us;{b} therefore our reason is unconquered.”

notes.text: The Greek of v. 7 is obscure, and the rendering is uncertain.
Or “the guards who stand before us are not the tyrant’s but those of the divine law”; the sense is uncertain.

verses.text: When this one too had died a blessed death, thrown into a cauldron, the seventh came forward, the youngest of all.{a}
The tyrant felt pity for him, although he had been terribly reviled by his brothers;
and seeing him already wrapped in chains, he had him brought nearer and tried to win him over, saying,

“You see the end of your brothers’ folly; for because of disobedience they have been racked to death. As for you, if you are not persuaded, you will be tortured miserably and will die before your time.
But if you are persuaded, you will be my Friend and will be a leader in the affairs of the kingdom.”
And while urging these things, he sent for the boy’s mother, so that, pitying her bereaved of so many sons, she might spur the survivor to become obedient and be saved.
But his mother urged him on in the Hebrew tongue,{b} as we will relate shortly afterward; and
he said, “Unbind me; let me speak to the king and to all his Friends with him.”
And overjoyed at the boy’s announcement, they quickly loosed him.
And running to the nearest of the frying pans,
he said, “Unholy tyrant, most ungodly of all the wicked, were you not ashamed, after receiving good things and the kingdom from God, to kill his servants and to rack those who practice piety?
For this, divine justice is storing you up for a more relentless and eternal fire and tortures, which throughout all eternity will not let you go.

Were you not ashamed, you most brutish creature, being a man yourself, to cut out the tongues of those who share your feelings and are made of the same elements, and to abuse and torture them in this way?
But they, dying nobly, fulfilled their piety toward God, whereas you will lament wretchedly for having killed without cause the contenders for virtue.”{c}
Then, being himself about to die, he said,
“I do not desert the testimony{d} of my brothers.
I call upon the God of our fathers to become merciful to my race;
but on you he will bring retribution in the life you now live and after your death as well.”
And having uttered this prayer, he flung himself down into the frying pans, and so gave up his life.{e}

notes.text: Swete prints “thrown into a cauldron” with a misplaced verse mark. The account of the seventh brother differs from 2 Macc 7:24–40.
Greek “the Hebrew voice,” probably meaning Aramaic or Hebrew; compare 16:15.
Swete divides v. 14 into two verses (12:14–15), so that the verses after it are numbered one higher than here.
Greek martyria, “witness” or “testimony.”
Literally “and so he gave it back.” Swete numbers this verse 12:20.

verses.text: If, then, the seven brothers despised sufferings even to death, it is agreed on every side that devout reason is sole master of the passions.
For if they had been slaves to the passions and had eaten defiling food, we would say that these had defeated them.
But in fact it was not so; rather, by the reason that is praised before God they prevailed over the passions.
And the supremacy of the mind cannot be overlooked, for they mastered both passion and pains.
How then can one fail to acknowledge the mastery of right reasoning over passion in these men, who did not turn back before the agonies of fire?{a}
For just as towers jutting out at harbors break the threatening waves and provide a calm anchorage for those sailing in,
so the seven-towered right reasoning of the young men, fortifying the harbor of piety, conquered the intemperance of the passions.
For having formed a sacred chorus of piety, they encouraged one another, saying,
“Brothers, let us die like brothers for the law; let us imitate the three young men in Syria{b} who despised the furnace that was a match for them.{c}
Let us not play the coward in the demonstration of piety.”
And one said, “Courage, brother!” and another, “Bear up nobly!”
And another said, “Remember where you came from, and by the hand of what father Isaac endured to be slain as a sacrifice for piety’s sake.”

Every one of them, and the whole band at once, gazing upon each other with bright faces and great boldness, declared, “With all our heart let us devote ourselves to the God who bestowed our souls, and let us lend our bodies to the guarding of the law.
Let us not fear him who thinks he kills;
for great is the struggle of the soul and the danger lying in eternal torment for those who transgress the commandment of God.
Let us arm ourselves, then, with the mastery over the passions that divine reason gives.
If we suffer like this, Abraham and Isaac and Jacob will receive us, and all the fathers will praise us.”
And to each one of their brothers as he was dragged away, those who remained said, “Do not put us to shame, brother, nor prove false to those who have died before us.”

You are not unaware of the bonds of affection of brotherhood, which the divine and all-wise providence has apportioned through the fathers to those begotten by them, and implanted through the mother’s womb.
In it the brothers dwell for the same length of time, are formed over the same period, are nourished from the same blood, and are brought to completion through the same life;
they are delivered after equal periods of time, and drink milk from the same springs, from which their brother-loving souls are nourished together in their mother’s embrace;
and they grow stronger still through being reared together, through daily companionship, through the rest of their education, and through our training in the law of God.
When the sympathy of brotherly love is so firmly established, the seven brothers held their harmony with one another with still deeper sympathy.
For being educated in the same law, practicing the same virtues, and brought up together in the just life, they loved one another all the more.{d}
For their common zeal for nobility strengthened their goodwill and harmony toward one another;
for together with piety it made their brotherly love more ardent.

But nevertheless, although nature, companionship, and virtuous habits were increasing the bonds of brotherhood for them, those who were left endured for piety’s sake, seeing their brothers being abused and tortured to death.

notes.text: The Greek sentence is grammatically incomplete; the rendering gives the probable sense.
That is, the three companions of Daniel (Dan 3), who were in Babylon; “Syria” is used loosely here for the eastern empire.
Or “the furnace equal in strength to them”; the sense of the Greek is uncertain.
Greek “they drew more to themselves”; the sense is uncertain.

verses.text: Beyond this, they even spurred each other on to the abuse, so as not merely to look down on their agonies but to rule over the passions that brotherly affection stirs.
O reasonings more kingly than a king and freer than the free!
O holy and well-tuned symphony of seven brothers on behalf of piety!
None of the seven youths turned coward or shrank back before death,
but all of them, as though running the road to immortality, hastened on to death through tortures.
For just as hands and feet move in concert with the soul’s guidance, so those holy youths, as though moved by the immortal soul of piety, were of one accord in going to death for its sake.
O all-holy sevenfold company of harmonious brothers! For just as the seven days of the world’s creation are arranged around piety,{a}
so the youths, dancing in chorus around the number seven, encircled it, bringing to nothing the fear of tortures.

We now shudder as we hear of the affliction of those young men; but they, not only seeing it, and not only hearing the immediate word of threat, but actually suffering it, endured, and that in agonies by fire.
And what could be more painful than this? For the power of fire, being sharp and swift, quickly dissolved their bodies.
And do not consider it a wonder that reason prevailed over those men in their tortures, since even a woman’s mind despised still more varied agonies.
For she who mothered the seven youths sustained the racking inflicted on every one of her children.
Consider how complex is the affection of love for children, drawing everything toward the sympathy felt in the inward parts.{b}
Even irrational animals have a sympathy and affection for their offspring like that of human beings.
For among birds, the tame ones that nest on the roofs of houses defend their nestlings,
and those that make their nests and hatch their young on mountain peaks, in clefts of ravines, and in holes and tops of trees also ward off anyone who approaches;
and if they cannot keep him away, they fly in circles around their young, anguished with love, calling out in their own voice, and help their children in whatever way they can.
Yet what need is there to show from beasts without reason how tenderly creatures feel for their young,
when even bees, at the season of making honeycomb, ward off those who approach, and strike those who come near their hive with their sting as with a sword,{c} and defend it even to death?
But sympathy for her children did not move the mother of the young men, whose soul was like that of Abraham.{d}

notes.text: Or “move in a circle about piety”; the image of vv. 7–8 is obscure, apparently relating the seven brothers to the seven days of creation and the Sabbath.
Greek splanchna, the inner organs regarded as the seat of feeling; here, the womb.
Greek “as with iron.”
Compare Abraham’s willingness to sacrifice Isaac (Gen 22), recalled in 16:20.

verses.text: O reasoning of sons, ruler absolute of passions! O godliness, dearer to a mother than her own offspring!{a}
Two things lay before the mother: piety, and the temporary safety of her seven sons according to the tyrant’s promise.
She loved piety more, which saves to eternal life in accordance with God.

O how can I describe in words the child-loving passions of parents, which stamp a wonderful likeness of soul and of form onto the small character of the child, especially since mothers are more sympathetic toward their offspring than fathers?
For the weaker in soul mothers are, and the more children they bear, the more they love their children.
Of all mothers, the mother of the seven loved her children most, she who through seven pregnancies had love for them planted in her,
and who, through her many birth pangs for each of them, was compelled to feel sympathy for them;
yet because of the fear of God she disregarded the temporary safety of her children.
More than this, the noble goodness of her sons and their readiness to obey the law made her tenderness for them all the greater.
For they were just, self-controlled, courageous, great-souled, loving toward their brothers, and so loving toward their mother that they obeyed her even to death in keeping the ordinances.

Nevertheless, though so many considerations connected with love of children were drawing the mother toward sympathy, in the case of none of them were the varied tortures able to turn her reason aside.
Rather, the mother urged them, each child singly and all of them together, on to death for the sake of piety.
O sacred nature and affection of parents, love toward offspring, nurture, and unconquerable passions of mothers!
Seeing them racked and burned one by one, the mother did not change her mind, because of piety.
She saw her children’s flesh melting in the fire, and the toes and fingers of their feet and hands quivering on the ground, and the flesh of their heads down to the chin laid out like masks.
O mother, tried now by bitterer pains than the birth pangs you suffered for them!
O woman, alone among women, who brought piety to birth whole and entire!
Your firstborn breathing his last did not turn you aside, nor the second looking piteously at you in his torments, nor the third expiring;
nor did you weep when you beheld the eyes of each one staring like a bull’s{b} at the same abuse in the torments, and their nostrils signaling their death.

When you saw the flesh of children severed upon the flesh of children, hands cut off upon hands, heads flayed upon heads, and corpses falling upon corpses, and saw the place crowded with your children’s bodies because of the tortures, you did not shed tears.
Not so do the melodies of the Sirens or the songs of swans{c} draw those who hear them to listen, as the voices of children calling to their mother in the midst of tortures.
How great and how many were the torments with which the mother was then tormented, while her sons were being tortured with wheels and with branding irons!
Yet reason grounded in piety, steeling her inmost being with manly courage amid the very passions, braced her to look past her love for her children, which was only for a time.
Although she saw the destruction of seven children and the intricate variety of the rackings, the noble mother, embracing them, let them go,{d} because of her faith toward God.
For as though seeing in her own soul, as in a council chamber, formidable counselors, nature and family and love of children and the racking of her children,
the mother, holding two votes, one bringing death and one bringing safety for her children,
did not choose the safety that would preserve seven sons for a short time,
rather, being a daughter of Abraham who revered God, she called to mind his steadfastness.
O mother of the nation, champion of the law, defender of piety, and winner of the prize in the contest of the heart!{e}
O more noble than males in fortitude, and more courageous than men in endurance!
For just as Noah’s ark, bearing the world in the world-engulfing flood, withstood the mighty waves,{f}
so you, guardian of the law, surrounded on every side by the flood of the passions and battered by the violent winds of your sons’ tortures, nobly withstood the storms that came because of piety.

notes.text: Swete prints vv. 1–2 as one verse.
Greek taurēdon, “with a bull-like glare.”
The Sirens of Greek legend lured sailors with their song; swans were said to sing beautifully before death.
Greek “having embraced, she released”; the sense is uncertain.
Greek splanchnon, “inward parts,” the seat of feeling.
Gen 6–8. “Noah” is associated with “rest” and “comfort” (Gen 5:29).

verses.text: If, then, a woman, an aged one at that, and the mother of seven children, endured seeing her children’s tortures even to death, admittedly devout reason is absolute ruler over the passions.
I have demonstrated, then, that not only have men prevailed over the passions, but a woman too has despised the greatest tortures.

And the lions around Daniel{a} were not so fierce, nor was the furnace of Mishael,{b} blazing with most violent fire, so burning, as was her nature of love for children set aflame as she saw her seven sons being tortured.
But by the reason of piety the mother quenched passions so many and so great.
For consider this also: if the woman had been faint of soul, mother though she was, she would have lamented over them, and perhaps she would have spoken thus:
“Ah, wretched me, and thrice unhappy many times over! I have borne seven children and have become the mother of none.
O seven pregnancies all in vain, seven ten-month carryings to no profit,{c} nursings without fruit, and sufferings in suckling!
In vain, my sons, did I endure many birth pangs for you, and the more grievous anxieties of rearing you.
Alas for my children, some of you unmarried, and those who married without profit! I shall not see your children, nor shall I be called blessed as a grandmother.
Alas, I who had many and beautiful children am a widow, alone and full of lamenting!
Nor, when I die, will I have any of my sons to bury me.”{d} But with no such lament did the holy and God-fearing mother mourn any of them,
nor did she try to turn any of them away from dying, nor did she grieve as though they were perishing.
But as though she had a mind of adamant, and were bringing the number of her sons to birth again into immortality, she rather urged them on with supplication to death for the sake of piety.
O mother, soldier of God for the sake of piety, aged and a woman! By your endurance you conquered even a tyrant, and in deeds and words you proved more powerful than a man.
For when you were arrested along with your children, you stood watching Eleazar being tortured, and you said to your children in the Hebrew language,{e}
“My children, a noble contest it is into which you have been summoned to testify on the nation’s behalf; strive in it with zeal for the law of our fathers.
For it would be shameful if this old man endured agonies for the sake of piety, while you, who are young, were terrified at the tortures.
Call to mind that it was by God’s doing that you received your portion of the world and had the enjoyment of life,
and therefore you ought to endure every pain for God’s sake.
For his sake also our father Abraham hastened to slaughter his son Isaac, the father of our nation; and Isaac, seeing his father’s hand bearing a sword descending upon him, did not cower.{f}
Daniel too, the just one, was cast among lions, and Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were flung as from a sling into a fiery furnace,{g} and for God’s sake they held out.
You, then, who have the same faith toward God, must not be dismayed.
For it would be unreasonable for those who know piety not to stand firm against pains.”
With these words the mother of seven, exhorting each one of her sons, persuaded them to die rather than transgress the commandment of God.
And they knew this also, that those who die for God’s sake live to God, as do Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the patriarchs.

notes.text: Dan 6. “Daniel” means “God is my judge.”
Dan 3. “Mishael” probably means “who is what God is?”
Pregnancy was commonly reckoned in antiquity as ten (lunar) months.
Greek “I will have none of my sons burying me”; where the lament ends is a matter of punctuation.
Compare 12:7. The language meant is probably Hebrew or Aramaic.
Gen 22. The Greek is ambiguous as to whether it is Abraham or Isaac who “did not cower.”
Dan 3; 6. “Hananiah” means “the LORD has been gracious” and “Azariah” “the LORD has helped.”

verses.text: Some of the guards also said that when she too was about to be arrested and executed, she hurled herself into the fire so that no one could touch her body.
O mother, who together with your seven sons broke down the violence of the tyrant, made void his evil designs, and displayed the nobility of faith!
For like a roof nobly set upon the pillars of your children, you bore without swaying the earthquake of the tortures.
Take courage, therefore, O mother of holy soul, holding firm the hope of your endurance toward God.
Not so majestic does the moon stand in heaven with the stars as you stand, honored before God, having lit the way to piety for your seven star-like sons; and you are fixed firmly in heaven with them.
For your childbearing was from Abraham the father.{a}

If it were permitted to us to paint, as an artist might, the piety of your story, would not those who looked on it shudder to see the mother of seven children enduring for piety’s sake various tortures even to death?
Indeed it would be fitting to inscribe on their very tomb these words also, as a memorial to those of our nation:
“In this place are laid to rest an old priest, a woman far on in years, and seven sons, through the brute force of a tyrant bent on overthrowing the Hebrews’ way of citizenship.
They also vindicated their nation, looking to God and enduring tortures even to death.”
For truly the contest in which they engaged was divine.
For on that day virtue presided over the games, testing them by endurance. The prize was incorruption in long-lasting life.
Eleazar led off the contest; the mother of the seven sons competed alongside; and the brothers fought on.
The tyrant contended against them; the world and all human life looked on.
Reverence for God was victor and crowned her own athletes.
Who did not marvel at the athletes of the true legislation? Who were not astonished?
The tyrant himself and his whole council marveled at their endurance,
because of which they now stand beside the divine throne and live the blessed age.
For Moses declares, “And all the holy ones are beneath your hands.”{b}
So these, made holy on God’s account, have been honored, and not with this honor alone, but also in this, that through them the foes gained no mastery over our nation,
and the tyrant was punished, and the homeland purified,

for they became as though a life paid in exchange for the nation’s sin.{c} And through the blood of those devout ones and their atoning death,{d} divine providence preserved Israel, which had previously been afflicted.
For Antiochus the tyrant, beholding the manliness of their virtue and how they held out amid the torments, held up their endurance before his troops as a model,
and he had them noble and courageous for infantry battle and for siege, and he ravaged and conquered all his enemies.{e}

notes.text: Greek “from Abraham the child,” probably meaning “from Abraham” with reference to the line descended from him; the phrase is obscure.
Deut 33:3 (Greek).
Greek antipsychon, “a life given in exchange.”
Greek hilastērion, “propitiatory” or “atoning”; the same word is used for the cover of the ark (the “mercy seat”) in Exod 25:17.
The Greek is abrupt; “them” apparently refers to his soldiers, who took the martyrs as their example.

verses.text: O Israelite children, offspring of the seed of Abraham,{a} obey this law and be devout in every way,
knowing that devout reason is master of the passions, and not only of pains from within but also of those from without.
Therefore those who gave over their bodies to pains for the sake of piety were not only admired by human beings but were also deemed worthy of a divine portion.
And because of them the nation obtained peace, and, renewing the observance of the law in the homeland, it took the enemies’ strongholds by siege.

And the tyrant Antiochus has been punished on earth and is being chastised now that he is dead. For since he was in no way able to compel the people of Jerusalem to live like foreigners and to abandon the way of life of their ancestral nations,{b}

he then departed from Jerusalem and marched against the Persians.
¶The righteous mother of the seven sons also spoke these words to her children:
“I was a pure virgin, and I never left my father’s house, but I kept watch over the rib that was built.{c}

No destroyer in the desert or seducer in the field corrupted me,{d} nor did the destroyer, the serpent of deceit, defile the purity of my virginity.{e} I remained with my husband through the time of my prime.
When these sons had grown to maturity, their father died. Happy was he! For having lived a life blessed with good children, he did not suffer the grief of the time of childlessness.
He, while yet among us, instructed you in the law and the prophets.
He read to us of Abel, slain by Cain,{f} of Isaac, offered as a burnt offering,{g} and of Joseph in prison.{h}
He spoke to us of Phinehas the zealot,{i} and to you he gave instruction concerning Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael amid the fire.
He glorified Daniel in the den of lions and called him blessed.
He reminded you of the scripture of Isaiah{j} that says, ‘Even if you pass through fire, the flame shall not burn you.’{k}
He sang to us David the hymn writer,{l} who says, ‘Many are the afflictions of the righteous.’{m}
He recited to us the proverbs of Solomon,{n} who says, ‘He is a tree of life to all who do his will.’{o}
He confirmed Ezekiel,{p} who says, ‘Shall these dry bones live?’{q}
For he did not forget the song that Moses taught, which teaches, ‘I will kill, and I will make alive.’{r}
This is your life and the length of your days.”{s}

O bitter was that day, and yet not bitter, when the bitter tyrant of the Greeks lit a fire under his savage cauldrons,{t} and in his seething fury hauled the seven sons of Abraham’s daughter to the catapult and then back again to his tortures,
pierced the pupils of their eyes, cut out their tongues, and put them to death with various tortures.
For these things divine justice pursued and will pursue the accursed wretch.
But the sons of Abraham, with their mother who won the prize, are gathered together into the place of their fathers, having received pure and immortal souls from God,
to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.

notes.text: “Abraham” is explained in Gen 17:5 as “father of a multitude.”
Greek “ancestral nations”; the sense is probably “ancestral customs.”
Gen 2:22, where the woman is “built” from the man’s rib; that is, she guarded her own body.
Compare Deut 22:25–27.

Gen 22.
Num 25:7–13. “Phinehas” is probably of Egyptian origin, perhaps meaning “the Nubian”; uncertain.
“Isaiah” means “the LORD is salvation.”
“David” is often explained as “beloved”; uncertain.
Ps 34:19 (Ps 33:20 in the Greek).
“Solomon” is related to the Hebrew word for “peace.”
Prov 3:18. The Greek “his will” is unclear; Proverbs speaks of wisdom.
“Ezekiel” means “God strengthens.”
